doc_title: DICGC deposit insurance: how your FD is protected
heading_path: DICGC deposit insurance: how your FD is protected > What DICGC insurance covers
text: Deposits in banks insured by the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) are protected up to ₹5 lakh per depositor, per bank, in the same right and capacity. This limit of ₹5,00,000 includes both the principal amount and the interest earned on it. So if you deposit ₹4,50,000 and it earns ₹30,000 interest, the full ₹4,80,000 is insured because it stays within the ₹5 lakh limit. In Hindi, this is called "बीमा सुरक्षा" — your paisa is protected even if the bank fails.

DICGC deposit insurance: how your FD is protected > What DICGC insurance covers
Deposits in banks insured by the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) are protected up to ₹5 lakh per depositor, per bank, in the same right and capacity. This limit of ₹5,00,000 includes both the principal amount and the interest earned on it. So if you deposit ₹4,50,000 and it earns ₹30,000 interest, the full ₹4,80,000 is insured because it stays within the ₹5 lakh limit. In Hindi, this is called "बीमा सुरक्षा" — your paisa is protected even if the bank fails.
publisher: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC), RBI subsidiary

doc_title: DICGC deposit insurance: how your FD is protected
heading_path: DICGC deposit insurance: how your FD is protected > What DICGC insurance covers > Which banks are covered
text: All commercial banks including public sector banks, private banks, foreign bank branches in India, regional rural banks, cooperative banks and Small Finance Banks are required to be DICGC members. Small Finance Banks like Suryoday, Ujjivan, Jana, Equitas and Utkarsh are scheduled commercial banks regulated by the RBI, so deposits held there are insured up to ₹5 lakh exactly like deposits in large banks. NBFCs, chit funds and companies accepting deposits are NOT covered by DICGC.

doc_title: DICGC deposit insurance: how your FD is protected
heading_path: DICGC deposit insurance: how your FD is protected > What DICGC insurance covers > What is not covered
text: Deposits above ₹5 lakh per bank are not insured; money in the same bank held in different branches still counts as one depositor for the ₹5 lakh limit, but different ownership types (single account, joint account) count separately. Deposits of foreign governments, inter-bank deposits and funds received outside India are not covered.

doc_title: DICGC deposit insurance: how your FD is protected
heading_path: DICGC deposit insurance: how your FD is protected > What DICGC insurance covers > When you get paid
text: If a bank is placed under moratorium or cancellation of licence, DICGC pays insured deposits within 90 days. Since the Deposit Insurance Act amendment of 2021, depositors do not need to file a claim — payment is processed through the bank's records directly. After the July 2024 amendment, DICGC must also pay an interim amount within 45 days of moratorium.

text: Only interest accrued up to the date the bank's licence is cancelled or moratorium is declared is counted inside the ₹5 lakh insurance limit. Interest accrued after that date is not insured.

doc_title: Fixed deposit basics: what an FD is and what the rate means
heading_path: Fixed deposit basics: what an FD is and what the rate means > What is a fixed deposit
text: A fixed deposit (FD) is an agreement where you deposit a lump sum with a bank for a fixed period (tenor, for example 12 months) and the bank pays you interest at a rate agreed at the start. The rate does not change during the tenor. In Hindi: "aap paisa bank mein lock karte ho, aur bank aapko pakka kamai deti hai". The amount you start with is the principal; the extra money you receive is interest.

publisher: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) — customer information

doc_title: Fixed deposit basics: what an FD is and what the rate means
heading_path: Fixed deposit basics: what an FD is and what the rate means > What is a fixed deposit > What "p.a." means
text: "p.a." stands for "per annum", meaning per year. When a bank advertises 8.50% p.a., it means the deposit earns 8.50% interest for one full year. If you lock money for only 6 months, you earn roughly half of the annual rate for that period (actual bank rules for part-period interest apply). The rate is applied to the principal you deposited.

doc_title: Fixed deposit basics: what an FD is and what the rate means
heading_path: Fixed deposit basics: what an FD is and what the rate means > What is a fixed deposit > Minimum and maximum deposit
text: Each bank sets its own minimum (for example ₹1,000 at many Small Finance Banks) and often a maximum for the advertised rate slab. Rates differ by tenor bucket: 7–45 days, 46–90 days, 91 days–1 year, above 1 year, and so on. The advertised "best rate" usually applies to one specific tenor bucket only, commonly 12 months.

doc_title: Fixed deposit basics: what an FD is and what the rate means
heading_path: Fixed deposit basics: what an FD is and what the rate means > What is a fixed deposit > Interest payout vs reinvestment
text: Non-cumulative FDs pay interest out to you monthly, quarterly or annually — useful if you want regular income ("har mahine kamai"). Cumulative FDs (reinvestment) add the interest back to the principal, so the final maturity amount is larger. Banks quote the annualised effective yield for cumulative deposits, which looks higher than the headline p.a. rate because of compounding.

doc_title: Compounding and maturity amount: how your money grows
heading_path: Compounding and maturity amount: how your money grows > How compounding works
text: Compounding means interest is calculated not only on your principal but also on interest already added. If an FD compounds quarterly, the bank computes interest every 3 months and adds it to the balance, so the next quarter's interest is earned on a slightly bigger amount. More frequent compounding gives a slightly higher final amount at the same headline rate.

publisher: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) — deposit interest compounding guidance

doc_title: Compounding and maturity amount: how your money grows
heading_path: Compounding and maturity amount: how your money grows > How compounding works > The maturity formula
text: For a cumulative FD: Maturity = P × (1 + r/n)^(n×t), where P is principal, r is the annual rate as a decimal, n is the number of compounding periods per year (4 for quarterly), and t is tenor in years. Example: ₹1,00,000 at 8.50% p.a. compounded quarterly for 1 year gives ₹1,00,000 × (1.085/4)^4 ≈ ₹1,08,839. A simple non-compounded calculation would give only ₹1,08,500, so quarterly compounding added about ₹339 extra.

section: Quarterly compounding is the common default
text: Most Indian banks, including Small Finance Banks, compound FD interest quarterly. The effective yield is therefore a little above the headline rate: 8.50% p.a. compounded quarterly is about 8.77% effective annual yield. Advertisements sometimes show this higher effective yield, so compare the quoted rate, not just the yield.

doc_title: Premature withdrawal: breaking your FD early
heading_path: Premature withdrawal: breaking your FD early > You can always break an FD early
section: You can always break an FD early
text: Indian banks must allow premature withdrawal of a term deposit at the request of the depositor, per the RBI's Fair Practices Code. "Premature withdrawal" means closing the FD before the chosen tenor ends — in Hindi, "FD ko beech mein todna". Money is never fully locked; the cost is a lower effective interest earned.

doc_title: Premature withdrawal: breaking your FD early
heading_path: Premature withdrawal: breaking your FD early > You can always break an FD early > How the penalty is calculated
text: When you break an FD early, the bank pays interest at the rate applicable for the period the money actually stayed deposited, minus a penalty (commonly 0.50% to 1.00%). Example: you booked a 12-month FD at 8.50% p.a. but broke it after 6 months. If the bank's 6-month rate is 7.50%, you get 7.50% − 0.50% penalty = 7.00% p.a. for those 6 months, not the 8.50% you booked.

Whether partial withdrawal is allowed depends on the bank's terms; many Small Finance Banks permit it once per FD.

doc_title: Tax on FD interest and TDS rules
heading_path: Tax on FD interest and TDS rules > FD interest is fully taxable
text: Interest earned on fixed deposits is taxed as income from other sources, added to your total income and taxed at your income-tax slab rate. There is no separate special rate for FD interest. In Hindi: "FD ki kamai par bhi tax lagta hai, aapki salary slab ke hisaab se".

publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

doc_title: Tax on FD interest and TDS rules
heading_path: Tax on FD interest and TDS rules > FD interest is fully taxable > TDS: when the bank cuts tax at source
section: TDS: when the bank cuts tax at source
text: Banks deduct Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) under Section 194A when total interest from that bank exceeds the threshold in a financial year. From 1 April 2025, the threshold is ₹50,000 for general customers and ₹1,00,000 for senior citizens per bank per year (raised by the Finance Act 2025 from the earlier ₹40,000/₹50,000). TDS is deducted at 10% if PAN is linked; without PAN, 20%.

doc_title: Tax on FD interest and TDS rules
heading_path: Tax on FD interest and TDS rules > FD interest is fully taxable > Form 15G and 15H
text: If your total income is below the taxable limit, you can submit Form 15G (Form 15H for senior citizens aged 60+) to the bank each financial year, and the bank will not deduct TDS on your interest. This only stops deduction at source; if your income later turns out to be taxable, you still owe the tax when filing your return.

doc_title: Tax on FD interest and TDS rules
heading_path: Tax on FD interest and TDS rules > FD interest is fully taxable > Different banks, separate limits
text: The ₹50,000 (or ₹1,00,000) TDS threshold applies per bank, per PAN. Depositing in several banks means each bank applies its own threshold. Interest from cooperative banks and all branches of one bank are counted together for that bank.

heading_path: Tax on FD interest and TDS rules > FD interest is fully taxable > Reporting in the tax return
text: Even if TDS was deducted, you must report FD interest in your annual return. TDS already deducted appears in Form 26AS and is credited against your final tax liability.

doc_title: Section 80TTB: tax deduction for senior citizens on deposit interest
heading_path: Section 80TTB: tax deduction for senior citizens on deposit interest > What Section 80TTB gives
text: Under Section 80TTB of the Income-tax Act, resident senior citizens (aged 60 or above) can deduct up to ₹50,000 of interest income earned from bank deposits — including fixed deposits and savings accounts — from their taxable income each financial year. In Hindi: "60 saal se upar waalo ke FD interest par ₹50,000 tak ki chhoot".

doc_title: Senior citizen FD rates: the extra interest advantage
heading_path: Senior citizen FD rates: the extra interest advantage > Extra 0.50% is the market norm
text: Most Indian banks pay senior citizens (age 60+) an additional 0.50% p.a. over the regular FD rate for the same tenor. Some banks extend a higher bonus (0.60%–0.75%) or a super-senior slabs (80+ extra) at their discretion; RBI rules do not fix the quantum, banks announce it in their rate cards.

doc_title: Small Finance Banks: are they safe?
heading_path: Small Finance Banks: are they safe? > What a Small Finance Bank is
section: What a Small Finance Bank is
text: Small Finance Banks (SFBs) — for example Suryoday, Ujjivan, Jana, Equitas and Utkarsh — are scheduled commercial banks licensed by the Reserve Bank of India. They are banks in the full legal sense, not NBFCs or microfinance companies. They were created to serve small borrowers and depositors who are underserved by large banks.

doc_title: Small Finance Banks: are they safe?
heading_path: Small Finance Banks: are they safe? > What a Small Finance Bank is > Same regulation, same insurance
text: SFBs are regulated by RBI exactly like other commercial banks: they follow RBI's exposure norms, capital rules and deposit regulations. Deposits with SFBs are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, same as any large bank. So a ₹5 lakh FD in an SFB carries the same insurance protection as in a big bank.

doc_title: Small Finance Banks: are they safe?
heading_path: Small Finance Banks: are they safe? > What a Small Finance Bank is > Why their rates are higher
text: SFBs advertise higher FD rates (often 0.50%–1.50% above large banks) because they lend to smaller borrowers at higher yields and want deposit growth. The higher rate is a business model feature, not a sign of illegality — but rate-chasing beyond the insured limit increases your exposure to that single bank.

doc_title: Small Finance Banks: are they safe?
heading_path: Small Finance Banks: are they safe? > What a Small Finance Bank is > Practical safety rule
text: Because insurance stops at ₹5 lakh per bank, the common rule of thumb is: keep the total (principal + interest) with any single bank within ₹5 lakh, and spread larger amounts across different banks. Within the insured limit, an SFB deposit is as protected as a public-sector bank deposit.

doc_title: Nomination and KYC for fixed deposits
heading_path: Nomination and KYC for fixed deposits > Nomination: name a nominee
text: Banks strongly recommend (and RBI requires banks to offer and record) nomination on every deposit account. A nominee is the person who receives the deposit money if the depositor dies. You can nominate one person per FD, and change the nominee any time by written request. In Hindi: "nominee wo insaan hai jo FD ka paisa lega agar aap na ho".

doc_title: Nomination and KYC for fixed deposits
heading_path: Nomination and KYC for fixed deposits > Nomination: name a nominee > Nomination is not a will substitute
section: Nomination is not a will substitute
text: A nominee holds the money on behalf of the legal heirs; nomination does not override succession law, but it makes the payout fast and avoids the bank waiting for a succession certificate for small amounts. Keeping nomination updated on every FD is the single easiest step to protect your family's access to the money.

doc_title: Nomination and KYC for fixed deposits
heading_path: Nomination and KYC for fixed deposits > Nomination: name a nominee > KYC documents needed
text: To open an FD you need KYC (Know Your Customer) proof: officially valid documents such as Aadhaar, PAN card, passport, voter ID or driving licence, plus a photograph. PAN is mandatory for deposits of ₹50,000 or more; without PAN, TDS is deducted at 20% instead of 10% on interest.

doc_title: Cumulative vs monthly-payout FDs: choosing how interest is paid
heading_path: Cumulative vs monthly-payout FDs: choosing how interest is paid > Two ways to receive interest
text: A non-cumulative (payout) FD pays interest to you at regular intervals — monthly, quarterly or annually — while the principal stays intact until maturity. A cumulative (reinvestment) FD does not pay anything during the tenor; interest is added back to the deposit and the full amount is paid at maturity. In Hindi: "har mahine kamai chahiye to payout FD, poori rakam end mein chahiye to cumulative FD".

doc_title: Cumulative vs monthly-payout FDs: choosing how interest is paid
heading_path: Cumulative vs monthly-payout FDs: choosing how interest is paid > Two ways to receive interest > Who should pick payout
text: Choose monthly or quarterly payout if you need the FD for regular household income — common for retirees replacing a salary. The payout amount equals the simple interest for the period: ₹1,00,000 at 8.50% p.a. pays ₹2,125 per month (approximately, monthly payout often uses simple interest divided by 12).

text: Banks often advertise the effective annualised yield of cumulative FDs, which is higher than the quoted p.a. rate. When comparing two banks, always compare the quoted p.a. rate and the compounding frequency, or compute the maturity amount for both.
